question: According to the Do Not Load table, poison (Division 6.1 or 2.3 poison inhalation hazard) materials must not be loaded with animal or human food unless what condition is met?
choice_a: The poison package is over-packed in an approved way
choice_b: The food is in a sealed metal container
choice_c: The vehicle has a separate compartment
choice_d: The driver has special hazmat food-handling training
explanation: The manual states poison materials cannot be loaded with animal or human food unless the poison package is over-packed in an approved way.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-11

question: According to the Do Not Load table, charged storage batteries must not be loaded in the same vehicle with which hazard class?
choice_a: Division 1.1 explosives
choice_b: Class 9 miscellaneous hazardous materials
choice_c: Class 7 radioactive materials
choice_d: Division 4.1 flammable solids
explanation: The Do Not Load table lists Division 1.1 explosives as not to be loaded with charged storage batteries.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-12

question: Under the Do Not Load table, Division 6.1 (Cyanides or cyanide mixtures) must not be loaded with what type of materials?
choice_a: Acids, corrosive materials, or other acidic materials which could release hydrocyanic acid
choice_b: Any flammable liquids regardless of type
choice_c: Refrigerated food products
choice_d: Empty cargo tanks
explanation: The manual states cyanide or cyanide mixtures must not be loaded with acids, corrosive materials, or other acidic materials that could release hydrocyanic acid, giving examples like Silver Cyanide and Sodium Cyanide.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-12

question: The manual states that mixed loads regulations require some hazardous products to be loaded in what manner?
choice_a: Separately, not together in the same cargo space
choice_b: Only in refrigerated compartments
choice_c: Stacked with heaviest items on top
choice_d: In portable tanks only
explanation: The manual states that the rules require some products to be loaded separately and cannot be loaded together in the same cargo space, as shown in Figure 9.9.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-12

question: According to the manual, the total transport index of all Class 7 (Radioactive) packages in a single vehicle must not exceed what number?
explanation: The manual states the total transport index of all packages in a single vehicle must not exceed 50.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-11

question: What is the difference between a cargo tank and a portable tank as described in the manual?
choice_a: Cargo tanks are permanently attached to a vehicle; portable tanks are loaded and unloaded off the vehicle
choice_b: Cargo tanks are only for gases; portable tanks are only for liquids
choice_c: Cargo tanks are smaller than portable tanks
choice_d: There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable
explanation: The manual states cargo tanks are bulk packaging permanently attached to a vehicle and remain on it when loaded/unloaded, while portable tanks are not permanently attached and are loaded/unloaded off the vehicle then placed on it for transport.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-12

question: On a portable tank with a capacity of more than 1,000 gallons, how tall must the letters of the shipping name be?
choice_a: At least two inches tall
choice_b: At least one inch tall
choice_c: At least four inches tall
choice_d: At least six inches tall
explanation: The manual states the letters of the shipping name must be at least two inches tall on portable tanks with capacities of more than 1,000 gallons, and one inch tall on tanks with capacities of less than 1,000 gallons.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-12

question: While a qualified person is watching the loading or unloading of a cargo tank, how far away from the tank may they be?
choice_a: Within 25 feet of the tank
choice_b: Within 50 feet of the tank
choice_c: Within 100 feet of the tank
choice_d: Any distance, as long as it is on the same property
explanation: The manual states the person watching loading or unloading of a cargo tank must be within 25 feet of the tank.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-12

question: Before moving a cargo tank of hazardous materials, what must a driver do regarding manholes and valves?
choice_a: Close all manholes and valves, no matter how small the amount in the tank
choice_b: Only close valves if the tank is more than half full
choice_c: Leave manholes open for ventilation during short moves
choice_d: Close manholes but valves may remain open if empty
explanation: The manual states you must close all manholes and valves before moving a tank of hazardous materials, no matter how small the amount in the tank or how short the distance.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-12

question: Before loading or unloading flammable liquids, what must a driver do with the engine?
choice_a: Turn off the engine, and only run it if needed to operate a pump
choice_b: Leave the engine running at idle at all times
choice_c: Rev the engine to test for leaks
choice_d: Turn off the engine only if the tank is more than half full
explanation: The manual states to turn off your engine before loading or unloading any flammable liquids, and only run the engine if needed to operate a pump.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-12

question: According to the manual, when should liquid discharge valves on a compressed gas tank be open?
choice_a: Only when loading and unloading
choice_b: At all times during transport
choice_c: Only when the engine is running
choice_d: Only during inspections
explanation: The manual instructs to keep liquid discharge valves on a compressed gas tank closed except when loading and unloading.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-12

question: How close to the traveled part of the road may you park a vehicle with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives?
choice_a: Never within five feet of the traveled part of the road
choice_b: Never within fifty feet
choice_c: Never within one mile
choice_d: It is always prohibited to park such a vehicle
explanation: The manual states never park with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives within five feet of the traveled part of the road.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-12

question: Except for brief periods needed for vehicle operation necessities like fueling, how far must a vehicle carrying Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives stay from a bridge, tunnel, building, place where people gather, or open fire?
choice_a: 300 feet
choice_b: 100 feet
choice_c: 500 feet
choice_d: 1,000 feet
explanation: The manual states not to park within 300 feet of a bridge, tunnel, building, a place where people gather, or an open fire, except for brief necessary periods like fueling.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-12

question: To satisfy the requirement of attending a placarded vehicle, a person must be in the vehicle awake and not in the sleeper berth, or within what distance with the vehicle in clear view?
choice_a: Within 100 feet of the vehicle
choice_b: Within 25 feet of the vehicle
choice_c: Within 500 feet of the vehicle
choice_d: Within 10 feet of the vehicle
explanation: The manual states the person attending a placarded vehicle must be in the vehicle, awake, and not in the sleeper berth, or within 100 feet of the vehicle and have it within clear view.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-13

question: If your vehicle breaks down while loaded with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives, what should you NEVER use as a stopped vehicle signal?
choice_a: Burning signals, such as flares or fuses
choice_b: Reflective triangles
choice_c: Red electric lights
choice_d: Hazard flashers
explanation: The manual warns never to use burning signals, such as flares or fuses, around a tank used for Class 3 or Division 2.1 materials, or a vehicle loaded with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives; use reflective triangles or red electric lights instead.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-13

question: If transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives, what must a driver have and follow?
choice_a: A written route plan
choice_b: A verbal agreement with the shipper only
choice_c: No special plan is required
choice_d: A GPS tracking device only
explanation: The manual states that if transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives, you must have a written route plan and follow that plan, prepared in advance by the carrier or by the driver if picking up explosives elsewhere.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-13

question: How close may a driver smoke to a placarded cargo tank used for Class 3 (flammable liquids) or Division 2.1 (gases)?
choice_a: Smoking is not allowed within 25 feet
choice_b: Smoking is not allowed within 10 feet
choice_c: Smoking is allowed if the windows are down
choice_d: Smoking is not allowed within 50 feet
explanation: The manual states do not smoke within 25 feet of a placarded cargo tank used for Class 3 (flammable liquids) or Division 2.1 (gases).
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-13

question: What must a driver do before fueling a motor vehicle containing hazardous materials?
choice_a: Turn off the engine, and have someone at the nozzle controlling fuel flow
choice_b: Leave the engine running to power the pump
choice_c: Disconnect the trailer from the tractor
choice_d: Notify the shipper by phone
explanation: The manual states to turn off your engine before fueling a motor vehicle containing hazardous materials, and someone must always be at the nozzle, controlling fuel flow.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-14

question: How far before the nearest rail must a driver stop when required to stop at a railroad crossing while carrying hazardous materials?
choice_a: 15 to 50 feet before the nearest rail
choice_b: 5 to 10 feet before the nearest rail
choice_c: 100 to 150 feet before the nearest rail
choice_d: Exactly 25 feet before the nearest rail
explanation: The manual states you must stop 15 to 50 feet before the nearest rail, proceeding only when sure no train is coming.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-14

question: When behind the wheel, where must a driver keep hazardous materials shipping papers?
choice_a: Within reach with the seat belt on, or in a pouch on the driver's door
choice_b: Locked in the glove compartment
choice_c: In the sleeper berth
choice_d: In the trailer with the cargo
explanation: The manual states that when behind the wheel, keep shipping papers within your reach (with your seat belt on), or in a pouch on the driver's door, so they can be easily seen by someone entering the cab.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-14

question: At the scene of a crash or incident involving hazardous materials, what is a professional driver's job?
choice_a: Keep people away from the scene and communicate the danger to emergency response personnel
choice_b: Attempt to clean up the spill personally
choice_c: Move the vehicle immediately to a repair shop
choice_d: Wait inside the vehicle until police arrive
explanation: The manual states a driver's job at a crash or incident scene is to keep people away, limit the spread of material only if safe, communicate the danger to responders, and provide shipping papers and emergency response information.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-15

question: According to the manual, should a driver fight a hazardous materials fire?
choice_a: No, unless the driver has the training and equipment to do so safely
choice_b: Yes, always, using the vehicle's fire extinguisher
choice_c: Yes, but only if the fire is small
choice_d: No, drivers are never permitted to use a fire extinguisher on truck fires
explanation: The manual states that unless you have the training and equipment to do so safely, don't fight hazardous materials fires, since dealing with them requires special training and protective gear.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-15

question: Before opening trailer doors when you suspect a fire, what should you do and why?
choice_a: Feel the doors to see if they are hot; if hot, do not open them because air may make the fire flare up
choice_b: Open the doors immediately to let smoke escape
choice_c: Spray water on the doors before opening
choice_d: Kick the doors open to check for damage
explanation: The manual instructs feeling trailer doors to see if they are hot before opening; if hot, you may have a cargo fire and should not open the doors, since opening lets air in and may make the fire flare up, whereas without air many fires only smolder.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-15

question: Why does the manual warn against trying to identify a leaking hazardous material by its smell?
choice_a: Toxic gases can destroy your sense of smell and can injure or kill you even if they don't smell
choice_b: It is a waste of time since smell never indicates the material
choice_c: It could alert bystanders to the danger unnecessarily
choice_d: It is illegal under federal law to smell chemicals
explanation: The manual warns not to try to identify the material or find the source of a leak by smell, because toxic gases can destroy your sense of smell and can injure or kill you even if they don't smell.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-15

question: If hazardous materials are spilling from your vehicle, what four steps does the manual say to take?
choice_a: Park it, secure the area, stay there, and call for help or send someone else for help
choice_b: Drive to the nearest phone, call the shipper, wait for instructions, then continue the route
choice_c: Unload the cargo yourself, repack the leaking container, and continue driving
choice_d: Notify only the consignee and continue to the delivery point
explanation: The manual lists park it, secure the area, stay there, and call for help or send someone else for help as the steps if hazardous materials are spilling from your vehicle.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-16

question: If your vehicle has a breakdown or accident while carrying Class 1 explosives and separating vehicles involved in a collision, how far from the vehicles and occupied buildings should explosives be placed?
choice_a: At least 200 feet
choice_b: At least 50 feet
choice_c: At least 500 feet
choice_d: At least 20 feet
explanation: The manual states to remove all explosives before separating vehicles involved in a collision and place the explosives at least 200 feet from the vehicles and occupied buildings.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-16

question: If you are transporting a Class 3 flammable liquid and have a leaking cargo tank, what should you do?
choice_a: Never transport the leaking tank farther than needed to reach a safe place, and get off the roadway if you can do so safely
choice_b: Continue to the delivery point regardless of the leak
choice_c: Transfer the liquid to another vehicle on the public roadway immediately
choice_d: Wait for the leak to stop before moving the vehicle at all
explanation: The manual states never transport a leaking cargo tank farther than needed to reach a safe place, and to get off the roadway if it can be done safely, without transferring flammable liquid on a public roadway except in an emergency.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-16

question: According to the manual, at what estimated property damage amount must the National Response Center be notified of a hazardous materials incident?
choice_a: Exceeding $50,000
choice_b: Exceeding $5,000
choice_c: Exceeding $500,000
choice_d: Any amount, regardless of value
explanation: The manual lists estimated property damage exceeding $50,000 as one of the conditions requiring a call to the National Response Center.
source_note: Delaware CDL Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, Version 4.0, Release Date: February 2025, AAMVA Modernized Testing System), Delaware Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-17
